newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Markets, government applaud small Australian pay rise.
newsitem.headline: Markets, government applaud small Australian pay rise.

text.p: Australia's key wages regulator granted low-paid workers a A$10 (US$7.70) a week pay rise on Tuesday, but rejected a union claim for a 8.75 percent national pay rise, saying restraint was needed to keep inflation down.
Financial market analysts and the government applauded the decision, saying it would help lock in low inflation and boost jobs growth. Market interest rates fell on the news.
Unionists, however, said they were disappointed and angry at what they said was a mean-spirited decision that lacked courage.

The Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC), which regulates national wage agreements covering about a third of workers, announced its ruling on a union claim for a A$20 a week pay rise for the low paid and the 8.75 percent pay rise across all national wage agreements known as "awards".
The AIRC said any more than A$10 a week would have endangered the Reserve Bank of Australia's target of keeping core annual inflation at between two to three percent.
"Any increase greater than the one which we grant carries a risk, in our view, of leading to a rise in interest rates," the AIRC said in its 273 page report.

"In the current state of the economy, with a high and seemingly stationary unemployment rate (of 8.7 percent) and an inadequate growth rate, we are unwilling to take that risk," the seven-person commission said.
Financial markets immediately welcomed the rejection of the economy-wide pay rise and the A$10 a week increase, which was slightly below market expectations.
Short term interest rates and long bond yields fell on the news, which buoyed hopes for a fourth official rate cut in less than a year.

"It was a good result from the financial markets' perspective certainly. I think basically low inflation for the next year or so is now locked in," Commonwealth Bank Senior Economist Michael Blythe said.
"It will certainly put the Reserve Bank's mind at ease," said Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields.

The Reserve Bank had warned the AIRC that if the claim by the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) was granted in full, it would directly add at least 1.6 percent to Average Weekly Ordinary Time Earnings (AWOTE).

The AIRC agreed, adding that it thought the full union demands would have eventually boosted AWOTE by over two percent to about six percent, well above the 4.5 percent "line in the sand" deemed by the Reserve Bank to be too high.
The AIRC said officials had estimated its A$10 a week decision would add only 0.34 percent to AWOTE.
The conservative Liberal/National government, which has lobbied for a A$8 a week rise for the low paid and no across-the-board rise, also welcomed the deal.
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith, who has championed the cause of individual agreements that are not regulated by the AIRC, said it would boost jobs growth.
"This is a fair deal for low paid workers and its consistent with low inflation," Reith told reporters.
Unions, however, were less than impressed.
ACTU President Jennie George said the decision lacked courage and penalised those who had shown the greatest wage restraint over recent years.
The Textile, Clothing and Footwear Union said the commission's "mean spritidness" had let low-paid clothing workers down.
